item.title: Lake Disappointment: The Neuroscience of Feeling Let Down
item.description:
Emotions

Lake Disappointment: The Neuroscience of Feeling Let Down

What you see is what you get, but is it what you think you should have gotten?

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • The name “Lake Disappointment” captures a real human moment: expecting fresh water but finding a salt pan.
  • We don’t evaluate anything in isolation; rather, we compare things to our expectations around them.
  • The brain constantly generates predictions about the world and updates them in response to incoming data.

At the turn of the century, water determined everything in inland exploration. It decided where livestock could survive, which in turn limited how far expeditions could travel. For entire routes through the desert, fresh water decided whether it was worth leaving home at all.

When Frank Hann, the explorer who mapped large areas of Western Australia, finally reached a vast lake marked by promising rivers and geographical patterns, he hoped he had found a substantial freshwater source. Instead, he discovered an enormous salt pan, undrinkable and effectively useless as far as the expedition was concerned.

He named this body of water “Lake Disappointment.”

The name then went on to appear in maps and government records and persisted for more than a century. The lake was an official “disappointment” until Western Australia restored the traditional Martu name, Kumpupintil, in 2020.

Naming things, especially things that are important, sounds like a serious enterprise. Most of our surroundings have names that are either pompous or decidedly neutral, as though they emerged naturally alongside the terrain itself without a creative spark. “Lake Disappointment,” by contrast, carries traces of a real human moment: the excitement of finding the lake, and the petty name-calling when it turned out to be less than expected.

Prediction engines

Notice how the lake isn’t objectively disappointing. As far as bodies of water go, you’d be hard-pressed to find anything wrong with this one. But, as humans, we don’t evaluate anything in isolation. We evaluate things against an expectation: our idea about what a thing should look or behave like.

Hann felt let down by the lake because his prior experience in geography pointed toward it being a freshwater lake. The mismatch between that prediction and the salt pan was, by definition, disappointing.

In the 1990s, neuroscientist Wolfram Schultz and his colleagues discovered that dopamine-producing neurons in monkeys don’t respond to the size of a reward but to its surprise. The neurons fired strongly for unexpected rewards, ignored predictable ones, and plunged below baseline when an expected reward failed to appear. Schultz described this encoding as a “reward prediction error,” or what it means to precisely measure the gap between expectation and reality.

The brain is continuously updating itself based on surprises. Predictions and prediction errors are an important part of that learning, and a sudden drop in dopamine signals to us that we're about to encounter a teaching moment.

However, the work of neuroscientist Karl J. Friston and others proposes that prediction is not merely a specialized function of the brain—it may well be its core operating principle. In this way, perception itself becomes a process of continuous hypothesis testing. The brain is constantly generating predictions about the world and updating them in response to incoming sensory data.

How expectations feel

If you won an Olympic medal, do you think you’d be happier winning silver or bronze?

The answer seems obvious. Silver represents a higher achievement, so it should make people happier. Yet when psychologists Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey, and Thomas Gilovich analyzed the reactions of athletes at the 1992 Olympic Games, they noticed that bronze medalists were visibly, measurably happier than silver medalists, both immediately after their events and later on the podium.

The researchers attributed this to a psychological phenomenon called “counterfactual thinking,” or our tendency to imagine alternative outcomes to events that have already occurred. For the athletes, their emotional state wasn't determined by the objective achievement, but rather by the alternative they were comparing it to. The silver medalist almost won gold and became the champion, making a second-place finish feel like a loss. It isn't a literal, millisecond-level prediction error like the one in Schultz’s monkeys, but it operates on the exact same comparative logic: Our emotional reality is dictated by the gap between what actually happened and what we expected to happen.

The bronze medalist, on the other hand, is comparing their outcome to finishing fourth and going home empty-handed. Because their imagined alternative hovered on the boundary of total failure, stepping onto the podium felt like a massive relief.

Doch

Whether we are comparing reality to an imagined alternative or simply to our own past, we never evaluate the world from a blank slate.

Adaptation-level theory, developed by Harry Helson in 1948, proposed that perception is not anchored to absolute values but to a shifting baseline formed by prior experience. A warm room feels cold after a sauna. A modest salary feels inadequate in a room full of wealth. The same stimulus produces different experiences, depending on the reference point against which it is evaluated, meaning our expectation is continuously recalibrated by what counts as “good” or “bad.”

And just as we automatically calibrate to our physical environment, we constantly calibrate to each other. One of the clearest signs that expectations sit at the center of human cognition is how often they need to be corrected in conversation. Consider a simple exchange:

“You’re not coming.”
“Yes, I am.”

Some languages even compress the correction into a single word. For example, German uses doch, French uses si, or Swedish uses jo to say, “Contrary to what you think, it's true,” making the response in the previous example just one word:

“You're not coming.”
“Doch.”

We are, in other words, constantly managing expectations—not only our own, but each other’s. In human communication, we continuously repair mismatches between what we think is true and what we think others think is true. When Frank Hann realized the lake had salt water in it, his brain did exactly what it had evolved to do. But by choosing the name “Lake Disappointment,” he wasn’t just correcting a prediction error, he was leaving a monument to it.

item.title: Is Creatine the Next Big Thing for Brain Health?
item.description:
Cognition

Is Creatine the Next Big Thing for Brain Health?

Creatine shows promise for cognition, but the evidence is still emerging.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Creatine may support cognition when the brain is under stress, such as sleep deprivation or fatigue.
  • Evidence for memory and attention is promising, but results in healthy adults remain mixed.
  • Creatine is not yet proven to prevent cognitive decline or function as a reliable nootropic.
Creatine for brain health?
Source: Karen E. Todd, RD

Creatine monohydrate is one of the most extensively studied sports supplements, with strong evidence for improving performance during repeated, high-intensity exercise and supporting resistance-training adaptations. Now, it is being promoted well beyond the gym, for memory, mood, focus, and protection against cognitive decline.

The interest is understandable, but the science does not yet support treating creatine as a proven nootropic or brain-health supplement for healthy adults. The more accurate takeaway is that creatine is biologically plausible and promising in specific circumstances, but the human evidence remains early, mixed, and limited by small studies.

A 2026 narrative review by Darren G. Candow and colleagues, “Creatine Supplementation and the Brain: Have We Put the Cart Before the Horse?”, offers a useful, measured assessment of this question. The authors conclude that although creatine may support brain function under certain forms of metabolic stress, much more research is needed before broad cognitive or brain-health claims are justified.

The Biology Makes Sense

The adult brain represents roughly 2% of body mass but uses about 20% of the body’s energy at rest. Like muscle, it depends on ATP, the cell’s immediate energy source, to support its work.

Creatine helps buffer and regenerate ATP through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. In muscle, this system is especially important when energy demand rises rapidly during short, intense activity. In the brain, it may help cells manage fluctuating energy demands during situations such as sleep deprivation, mental fatigue, hypoxia, injury, or disease.

Preclinical research also suggests that creatine could affect processes relevant to brain health, including oxidative stress, neurotransmission, and cellular resilience. However, these mechanisms come largely from laboratory and animal research. They do not establish that creatine supplementation improves mood, memory, neuroprotection, or cognitive aging in people.

That distinction matters: a plausible mechanism is a reason to study a supplement, not proof that it works.

Where the Evidence Holds Up

The strongest signal so far appears to be in situations that place unusual demands on brain energy metabolism. Small studies suggest that creatine may help preserve some aspects of cognitive performance during sleep deprivation, mental fatigue, or hypoxia.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials involving 492 participants found small improvements in memory, attention time, and information-processing speed, but no statistically significant improvements in overall cognition or executive function. The authors emphasized the need for larger, more robust trials.

That evidence should be interpreted cautiously. The trials differed substantially in their participants, doses, study durations, cognitive tests, and research quality. A subsequent commentary also identified a methodological concern in the meta-analysis: multiple outcomes from the same participants may have been treated as independent observations, which can overstate the precision of the overall estimate.

Earlier reviews reached a similarly cautious conclusion. Creatine may improve short-term memory and reasoning in some healthy participants, but findings for attention, reaction time, executive function, long-term memory, mental fatigue, and other outcomes have been inconsistent. Results also appear less reliable in young, healthy, well-rested people.

In short, there is some evidence of potential benefit, but not enough to conclude that creatine reliably improves cognition in the average healthy adult.

Potential Clinical Uses

Creatine is also being studied in conditions associated with impaired brain energy metabolism, including major depressive disorder, mild traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s disease, and post-COVID fatigue.

These are important research areas, but the evidence remains preliminary. Studies are generally small, short, exploratory, or designed primarily to evaluate feasibility and safety rather than to establish clinical efficacy.

For example, a small pilot study in people with Alzheimer’s disease found that creatine supplementation was feasible and was associated with preliminary improvements in working memory and executive function. It was not designed to prove that creatine treats Alzheimer’s disease or slows cognitive decline.

The Measurement Challenge

An important limitation in this field is that researchers do not simply measure whether someone takes creatine and then assume that more reaches the brain. Brain creatine is commonly assessed with magnetic resonance spectroscopy, or MRS, a noninvasive imaging technique.

MRS is valuable, but results can vary based on the brain region measured, scanner and acquisition settings, signal quality, data processing methods, and the way findings are reported. These methodological differences make it difficult to compare results across studies.

Some studies have reported increases in brain creatine after supplementation, but the size of the increase varies considerably. Dose, duration, baseline creatine status, individual biology, transport into the brain, and the measurement method may all affect the response.

This creates a key unanswered question: even if supplementation raises brain creatine levels, does that change translate into meaningful improvements in memory, attention, mood, daily functioning, or long-term cognitive health?

We do not yet know.

What We Still Do Not Know

Several major uncertainties remain:

  • The optimal dose: Most studies have used 3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate daily, the same range commonly used in sports nutrition. It is not known whether higher doses, longer use, or both are necessary to consistently alter brain creatine levels or cognitive outcomes.
  • The optimal duration: Most cognitive studies have been short, often lasting days or weeks rather than years. There is little long-term evidence on whether creatine can prevent age-related cognitive decline or reduce dementia risk.
  • Who benefits most: People with lower baseline dietary creatine intake, including vegetarians and vegans, may be plausible candidates for study. Older adults and people experiencing sleep loss, mental fatigue, or impaired energy metabolism may also be more likely to benefit than young, well-rested adults.
  • Which outcomes matter: Researchers need adequately powered trials that measure outcomes people care about, not only laboratory cognitive tests, MRS findings, or mechanistic biomarkers.

A 2026 systematic review in older adults found limited but encouraging evidence for cognitive benefits, particularly in memory and attention. However, the review also concluded that higher-quality clinical trials are needed.

Bottom Line

Creatine monohydrate is a well-studied supplement for exercise performance, but it is not yet a proven brain-health supplement or nootropic.

The most defensible claim is that creatine may modestly support aspects of cognitive performance when the brain is under metabolic stress, such as during sleep deprivation or fatigue. Its roles in healthy aging, mood, neurodegenerative disease, brain injury, and long-term cognitive protection remain promising but unproven.

Creatine is generally well tolerated at customary doses in healthy adults, though people with kidney disease, chronic medical conditions, or questions about medications should speak with a clinician before using it. It can also raise blood creatinine levels, which may complicate interpretation of kidney-function testing.

For now, the foundations of brain health remain less glamorous but better supported: sufficient sleep, regular physical activity, cardiovascular risk-factor management, social and intellectual engagement, and a nutrient-dense dietary pattern. Creatine may eventually earn a place alongside those habits, but the evidence is not there yet.

item.title: Dysgraphia: Solving It Via Dyslexia
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Dysgraphia: Solving It Via Dyslexia

Dysgraphia is more than just bad handwriting.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Writing involves learning the code for mapping spoken to written language.
  • Dysgraphia is more than just bad handwriting and the latter may have different causes.
  • Dysgraphia arises from inefficiencies in the linguistic or other brain systems.

Sean, 9, can describe a groundhog's complex burrows in vivid detail. But ask him to write two sentences about it, and he freezes. He stalls. He erases, starts over, and stalls again. An hour later, he quits, with a hole in the middle of the paper.

This scenario plays out like Groundhog Day in countless households every evening. Parents press children like Sean to try harder. The evening inevitably ends with tears and angry words. Families are at a loss as to what to do until they stumble on the word "dysgraphia." Can it be dysgraphia?

What Is Dysgraphia, Exactly?

Developmental dysgraphia is often identified by a persistent discrepancy between a person’s actual vs. expected writing ability based on their age, instruction, and intelligence (Chung et al., 2020). Dysgraphia is a language-based learning disorder affecting written expression. With dysgraphia, the brain has difficulty translating thoughts into writing with the speed and accuracy expected at that age.

Let me illustrate. Figure 1 shows the building blocks of the linguistic system. Spoken language is made up of sounds, words, utterances, and discourse (stretches of talk). Correspondingly, written language comprises letters, written words, sentences, and text. While spoken language is acquired naturally, writing requires formal learning of the "code"—the mapping of sounds to letters, utterances to sentences, etc.

Mapping the spoken linguistic system to the written.
Source: Coral PS Hoh/Dysolve®

Therefore, any problem with any part of these building blocks or mapping can create challenges with written language. Written expression also demands efficient operation and coordination of other brain systems, including the sensory-motor, cognitive, psycho-social, and executive function systems, as shown in Figure 2 (Berninger & Richards, 2002). (These brain systems also affect other learning disabilities such as dyscalculia.)

Written expression requires coordinating several brain systems.
Source: Coral PS Hoh/Dysolve®

As with the other learning disabilities—dyscalculia (math) and dyslexia (reading)—dysgraphia presently lacks an established operational definition. An operational definition specifies exactly how the concept will be measured. In a previous post, I operationalized "dyslexia" as inefficiencies in the linguistic system in the brain, much of which also apply to dysgraphia. And like dyslexia, dysgraphia may affect an estimated 20% of the population (Chung et al., 2020).

Signs of Dysgraphia Change With Age

As writing demands increase with age, warning signs tend to shift from concrete, physical struggles in early childhood to more abstract, organizational challenges in adolescence. For example, kindergartners with dysgraphia may have difficulty copying letter shapes, middle schoolers keep misspelling simple words, while high schoolers struggle to take notes.

Why It's More Than Just Poor Handwriting

Dysgraphia does not look the same from person to person. This is because it can result from inefficiencies in different parts of the linguistic system or the other brain systems.

Many people think of dysgraphia as a handwriting problem, but this symptom is not always present. When it is, the reason may be found in motor skills or something else. For example, a child who has difficulty retaining words is compelled to copy them down letter-by-letter. Attending to each letter of the word takes away mental resources usually allocated to monitoring spacing, sizing, and visual alignment. The result is poor handwriting.

The Processing Problem With Written Language

Writing is one of the most demanding tasks at school. As illustrated above, it is a global task requiring the orchestration of many building blocks of language and multiple brain systems simultaneously. Writing is considerably more demanding than oral expression. While the child may be able to describe groundhog hibernation verbally, they may not be able to write it down. The problem lies in the machinery required to map spoken language to the written code and coordinating several brain systems to externalize their thoughts onto the page.

Dysgraphia and Dyslexia

Over a third of children with writing problems also have reading problems and vice versa (Chung et al., 2020). Reading difficulty involves language reception, whereas writing difficulty entails language production. The language processes activated for both overlap to a large extent, but production—the act of creation—is more demanding. This is why some students can read passably well but struggle with written composition.

Why Accommodations Alone Are Not Enough

Extended time, assistive technologies, shorter assignments, and testing through oral means—these accommodations make school life easier but do not address the underlying processing problem that made writing hard in the first place. It is important to distinguish between two major approaches: compensating for the difficulty vs. correcting the root problem.

Compensatory v. corrective approaches.
Source: Coral PS Hoh/Dysolve®

New Treatments for Dysgraphia

As new technologies enable us to reach into brain processes, new treatments for dysgraphia will likely involve finding the root problem in the brain, as is presently done for dyslexia. The evidence-backed method for dyslexia focuses on improving the efficiency of foundational language processes before instruction on reading skills begins. Similarly, assessment following the foundational training can determine remaining gaps that need to be filled to reach writing proficiency.
